title: Write the guide, then go spotting
allegory: Autointerp is like writing a field-guide entry for a mystery bird from its best photos, then handing only the entry to a birdwatcher with a fresh album: the entry counts only if they tick the right photos.
map: the top activating examples, firing tokens marked << >>
the field-guide entry written from them
a birdwatcher with only the entry and a fresh album
the scorer model: explanation plus held-out text, no activations
how many photos they tick correctly
the score: predicted versus real activations

cap.1: A model's insides hold tens of thousands of tiny detectors, each firing on something. Nobody can read examples for all of them by hand.
cap.2: Max-activating examples suggest what a latent means, but reading them for every latent in an SAE is hopeless. OpenAI's run covered all 307,200 neurons in GPT-2.
cap.3: Human inspection does not scale to SAE dictionaries. OpenAI (2023) automated it: GPT-4 explained each of GPT-2's 307,200 neurons, and each explanation was then scored.

cap.1: One helper writes a field-guide entry from the bird's best photos. A second helper, who never saw them, uses only the entry to tick birds in a fresh album.
cap.2: The explainer sees the top activating texts with firing tokens marked << >> and writes a short explanation. The scorer sees only that sentence and new texts.
cap.3: Explainer: k top sequences with activating tokens delimited, output capped at 20 words. Scorer: explanation plus held-out sequences, no activations; it predicts where the latent fires.

cap.1: Two halves, one loop: explain, then test the explanation. The test is what makes the label trustworthy.
cap.2: Explanation, then predictions, then a comparison with real activations. The score, not how nicely the sentence reads, is your measure of interpretability.
cap.3: Turning explanations into predictions makes them falsifiable. Scoring on held-out sequences judges the explanation on the latent's whole behaviour, not the examples it was fitted to.

chapters.name: The snow problem
chapters.verdict: Top examples are the extreme tail. Describe the whole range.

cap.1: If all the best photos happen to show snow, the guide says 'white bird in snow' and fails all summer. The best examples are not the typical ones.
cap.2: Top activating sequences are the extreme upper tail and share incidental context. The explanation describes the tail, so it can score near chance on fresh text.
cap.3: Sample across activation quantiles, include non-firing sequences so the boundary is visible, and keep the 20-word cap so the explainer cannot hedge with a word list.

chapters.name: Grading the graders
chapters.verdict: Use scores as evidence; never cite a label as fact.

cap.1: How do you grade a whole set of detectors? The usual ruler can be gamed. Autointerp scores are a second ruler: useful, but still only evidence.
cap.2: SAEs are usually judged on sparsity versus reconstruction, but feature absorption can improve sparsity while latents get harder to read. Autointerp scores add an independent check.
cap.3: Current practice: the sparsity/reconstruction Pareto frontier. Emerging: autointerp scoring as a separate axis. What you need: treat every label as a scored hypothesis, never a fact.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Dashboard labels come from this pipeline

cap.1: Every label on a model's parts is a guess until it predicts something. OpenAI's own run found most GPT-2 neurons got poor scores.
cap.2: Over a thousand of the 307,200 neurons scored 0.8 or better; the vast majority scored badly, and GPT-4 explained worse than people did. The same pipeline fills in Neuronpedia's dashboards.
cap.3: Labels shape what we believe models represent, and later what we steer. Insisting on the scoring half keeps both understanding and steering anchored to evidence.

caption.1: Top row: where the latent really fires on 8 fresh texts. Bottom row: the scorer's guesses from the explanation alone. Tap the bottom row to fix them.
caption.2: This is the scoring half. Watch 'caught' and 'false alarms', not just agreement. Clear most of the top row and see how well a lazy 'never fires' guess already agrees.
caption.3: Scoring compares simulated with true activations on held-out text. Raw agreement is inflated by the base rate of non-firing, so prefer a measure that rare firing cannot fool.

where_else: Model-graded scoring in evals: one model judging another, which needs its own checks
Activation oracles: pointing a language model at another model's internals to get English back
Science in general: a hypothesis earns trust by predicting held-out data, not by reading well

hamming.what: Using one language model to explain a latent from its top examples, and another to test that explanation by predicting activations on new text.
hamming.when: Whenever you label SAE latents or neurons at scale, or read a label on a dashboard such as Neuronpedia.
hamming.why: A label that reads well can still be wrong; only its predictions on held-out text show whether it captures what the latent actually does.

object.title: The prediction ledger
object.subtitle: Ten fresh texts in a row: how hard the latent really fires, beside what the explanation predicts.

knobs.label: explanation written from top only (0) or the full range (1)

cap.1: Ten fresh texts, strongest firing first. Left bars: how hard the latent really fires. Right bars: what the scorer predicts from the explanation.
cap.2: An explanation fitted only to the top examples predicts the top two texts and nothing else.
cap.3: A tail-fitted explanation's simulated activations match only the extreme quantile, so agreement over held-out text is poor.

cap.1: Along the rows, the middle texts fire moderately, and the explanation has nothing to say about them.
cap.2: Most of a latent's firings are mid-range, and a top-k prompt never showed any of them.
cap.3: The body of the activation distribution is missing from top-k prompts: the source of tail bias.

cap.1: Rewrite the entry from photos across the whole range, and the guesses follow the real bars.
cap.2: An explanation built from texts sampled across the range, plus some where it never fires, predicts the graded behaviour.
cap.3: Quantile-sampled prompts yield explanations whose simulations track the latent across its full distribution.

cap.1: From above, the two columns match. This explanation has earned its label.
cap.2: Only a scored explanation counts as evidence about what a latent means.
cap.3: Score, then cite: an explanation is a hypothesis validated by predictive agreement on held-out data.

predict.q: An explanation reads beautifully but scores near chance on fresh text. What is the likely cause?

options.t: It was written only from the top examples, the extreme tail
The scorer model is too small

predict.why: Top activating texts share incidental context, so the explanation describes the tail. Sample across the range and include texts where the latent does not fire.

predict.q: A latent fires on 1 text in 20. An explanation predicts 'never fires'. How often does it agree with the truth?

options.t: 95% of the time, while being useless

predict.why: Raw agreement rewards the base rate. Check what was caught and what was falsely flagged instead.

object.where: Anywhere a summary must earn its keep by predicting: field guides, diagnostic criteria, job descriptions tested on new hires.
